rationale:
This slate fits the quota: 3 long videos, 3 Shorts and 2 carousels. It follows the ~50/30/20 mix.

**Emerging and rising topics (about half the slate)**
- HRT pill vs patch (L1) and its Short (S2)
- Smartwatch calorie accuracy (S1)
- Scented cleaners and indoor air (S3)

**Evergreen topics with a timely hook (about 30%)**
- REM sleep, tied to the Gen X drinking news (L3)
- Walking pace vs step count (C1)
- Stroke in younger adults, with the BE-FAST warning signs (C2)

**Myth-busting (about 20%)**
- Mammogram overdiagnosis vs the Galleri blood test (L2). This also rides the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month in 5 days.
- S1 also works as a myth-buster: "your watch's calorie number is accurate."

**How the day is balanced**
- No body system gets three pieces. The day covers hormones/menopause, cancer screening, sleep, fitness tech, indoor air, exercise and stroke. Only L1 (clots) and C2 (stroke) touch the blood vessels.
- S2 is a spin-off of L1, our strongest trend (momentum 88), to drive viewers to the long video.

**Caution topics and what was left out**
- The radar rejected nothing. Three of today's picks are marked caution: HRT, mammograms and Galleri.
- Each gets an evidence-first angle: absolute risk alongside relative risk, one reanalysis rather than the final word, and a "talk to your clinician" frame.
- None of them tells viewers to switch, stop or buy anything.
- Two strong candidates are on hold for another day: the semaglutide heart analysis and the Gen X drinking study. Holding them keeps the mix balanced, and the alcohol angle already appears inside L3.

**Wording to watch in scripts**
- Scented cleaners are conference data, not a peer-reviewed paper yet. Say "still being studied" about health effects.
- The smartwatch study had only 58 participants. Say so on screen.
- The "strokes nearly doubled" figure is attributed to Neurology, but the radar's only link is a different JAMA Network Open paper on treatment after stroke. The C2 script should check the Neurology figure against the paper itself, or say "rising" if it can't be confirmed.

pieces.topic: Menopause HRT: oral pills vs transdermal patches/gels and blood clot risk (The BMJ, Danish nationwide study, 180k+ women)
pieces.angle: 'Pill or patch? The HRT question worth asking your doctor.' Put the absolute risk (~1 extra serious clot per 1,000 women per year on oral) next to the scary relative-risk headlines. Explain why the liver matters: oral estrogen passes through the liver first, which raises clotting factors, while transdermal largely doesn't. Cover what the study can and can't show (observational, case-control). Explain who the difference matters most for, e.g. people with existing clot risk factors. End with a list of questions to take to a clinician. Never tell viewers to switch or stop.
pieces.working_title: HRT Pill vs Patch: The Blood Clot Difference Nobody Explained to You
pieces.why: Highest momentum on the radar (88, climbing for 3 snapshots, peak in 3–10 days). Menopause is a core audience interest and no major creator has explained it yet. There is enough depth for 10+ minutes (mechanism, absolute vs relative risk, limitations, clinician questions).

pieces.topic: Mammogram overdiagnosis may be under 5%, not 30–50% (JNCI reanalysis of 8 RCTs), contrasted with the Galleri multi-cancer blood test missing its primary endpoint in the NHS trial
pieces.angle: 'Which cancer screens have the strongest evidence?' Part 1: the JNCI meta-analysis of all 8 mammography RCTs suggests overdiagnosis may be under 5%, much lower than the 30–50% often quoted. Present it as one strong reanalysis in a debate that isn't settled, and explain overdiagnosis and lead time. Part 2: Galleri. In the ~140k-person NHS-Galleri RCT (NEJM) it missed its primary endpoint (fewer stage III/IV cancers). It did show fewer stage IV diagnoses in later rounds. Cover false positives and cost. An FDA panel voted in favour, but that is not approval and not proof it cuts deaths. Existing guideline-recommended screening is still recommended. Close by telling viewers to talk to a clinician about age and personal risk. Suggested title: 'Mammograms vs the $949 Cancer Blood Test: What the New Evidence Actually Shows'.
pieces.working_title: The Mammogram Myth That Went the Other Way (and the $949 Blood Test That Didn't Deliver)
pieces.why: Myth-busting slot. Two caution topics handled evidence-first. Low competition, and Breast Cancer Awareness Month starts in 5 days, which will lift search demand. Pairing the two stories gives it long-form depth. | fact-check: Verified: Njor, Pedersen, Lynge, Smith, Rebolj, 'Breast cancer overdiagnosis in mammography trials—separating signal from noise: a meta-analysis', JNCI, 14 Sep 2026 (DOI 10.1093/jnci/djag302). It reanalysed all 8 RCTs and its results fit an overdiagnosis rate under 5%. Galleri verified: NHS-Galleri RCT (~140k; final results in NEJM, 22 Sep 2026) did not meet its primary endpoint, a significant cut in stage III/IV cases of 12 prespecified cancers. The trial did report 22% and 26% fewer stage IV diagnoses in screening rounds 2 and 3. The FDA advisory panel met on 23 Sep 2026. It voted 7–2 (1 abstention) that benefits outweigh risks and 6–4 on effectiveness. The panel's vote is not approval. Problems: 'the $949 Blood Test That Didn't Deliver' is too absolute, given the stage IV reduction and the panel's backing. That wording risks unfair framing and a defamation-style complaint. Check the exact n (142,942) and the $949 US list price against NEJM and GRAIL before using them. For balance, name the ongoing overdiagnosis debate (Cochrane/Nordic estimates) and note the JNCI analysis relies on Danish reference data. Never imply that people should skip screening. Sources: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260924020351.htm ; https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-09-analysis-overdiagnosis-breast-cancer-screening.html ; https://www.npr.org/2026/09/23/nx-s1-5978122/fda-blood-cancer-test-galleri ; https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-oncology/20260924/fda-panel-benefits-of-galleri-blood-test-for-multicancer-detection-outweigh-risks

pieces.topic: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases (PLOS Medicine, 95,559 UK Biobank wearers)
pieces.angle: 'REM sleep and 83 diseases: what a 95,000-person study can and can't tell you.' Explain what REM does. Present the findings as associations, with REM estimated from a wrist device by an algorithm. Use Parkinson's and dementia as the clear example of reverse causation: early disease can cut REM years before diagnosis. Cover what reliably reduces REM (alcohol, short sleep, irregular schedules), citing sleep-lab evidence. If you use the Gen X drinking stat, make it one clearly labelled aside ('separate data: heavy drinking at 50–64 rose >36%, 2018–2024'), not proof of a REM link. Say plainly that consumer trackers only estimate sleep stages, and don't encourage people to chase REM numbers. Finish with evidence-based habits and tell viewers to see a clinician about persistent sleep problems.
pieces.working_title: REM Sleep and 83 Diseases: What This Huge Study Really Means for You
pieces.target_keyword: how to get more REM sleep
pieces.why: Evergreen sleep topic refreshed with a big, timely study (momentum 76, 3 snapshots). Folding in the Gen X alcohol story adds a second trending hook without spending a separate slot on it. | fact-check: Verified: PLOS Medicine 2026, 'Accelerometer-derived real-world sleep stages and risk of incident diseases: A UK Biobank cohort study and phenome-wide association analysis' (doi 10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213). n=95,559, 7-day wrist accelerometer, sleep stages estimated by a deep-learning model (not EEG), median follow-up 8.9 years. Each IQR (47.6 min) more REM was linked to lower risk of 83 diseases, e.g. heart failure HR 0.74, dementia 0.54, Parkinson's 0.20. Issues: (1) The Parkinson's and dementia HRs very likely reflect reverse causation, since these diseases disrupt REM years before diagnosis. Use them as the example of reverse causation, not as a benefit claim. (2) Sleep stages came from a research-grade wrist accelerometer plus an algorithm, not from polysomnography. The stage estimates are themselves imperfect. (3) Gen X data is verified: Annals of Internal Medicine, NHIS, heavy drinking at ages 50–64 up >36% from 2018 to 2024. But it has nothing to do with REM or disease outcomes. Present it at most as one separate line of context, not as evidence that drinking is driving REM loss in this study. (4) The claim that alcohol suppresses REM needs its own sleep-lab source; there is well-established literature for it. (5) Limit habits to evidence-based sleep hygiene/CBT-I basics. Sources: https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1005213 ; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260923035930.htm ; https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/21/health/alcohol-use-decline-study-wellness

pieces.topic: Smartwatch calorie estimates off by 15–25% vs lab gold standard, with larger errors at higher body fat (PLOS One)
pieces.angle: 'Your watch's calories-burned number is a rough estimate.' In a small lab test (58 adults, 10 minutes of cycling), 4 popular smartwatches were off by a median of about 15–25% against a lab gas-analysis gold standard. Most overestimated, and the error grew at higher body fat. It's a small, short study, so treat it as a caution, not a verdict. Watches are better at tracking trends in steps and heart rate than exact calories. Don't extrapolate weekly calorie totals and give no eating instructions. Suggested title: 'How Accurate Is Your Smartwatch's Calorie Count? A Lab Test Checked'.
pieces.working_title: Should You Eat Back Your Apple Watch Calories? A Lab Test Says Think Twice
pieces.why: Published today with almost no creator coverage and low competition. Product-specific and visual, the kind of thing that spreads on TikTok and Shorts. Doubles as a myth-buster. | fact-check: Verified: PLOS One, published 29 Jul 2026, 'Body fat, skin tone, and the accuracy of smartwatch caloric expenditure estimates' (PubMed 42525581). n=58 Hispanic adults, one 10-minute recumbent-cycling protocol, compared with indirect calorimetry (COSMED K5). Devices: Apple Watch S8, Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung GW5, Garmin FR955. Median error was ~15–25%. Apple, Garmin and Samsung overestimated, and error grew with body fat. Problems: (1) The '1,200–2,400 kcal a week' figure is our own extrapolation from a 10-minute cycling test, not a study finding. Drop it. (2) 'Eat back your calories' framing pushes calorie-restriction advice at a broad audience, which is an eating-disorder risk. Reframe it as 'treat the number as a rough estimate'. (3) State the limits: one short cycling test, one population, 58 people. Sources: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0353261 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42525581/

pieces.topic: HRT pills vs patches: the '1 in 1,000' absolute risk behind the blood clot headlines
pieces.angle: A Danish registry study in The BMJ (women 50–69) linked oral HRT to a higher risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs. In absolute terms that's about [paper's figure] extra clots per 1,000 women per year. Patches and gels showed no overall increase in clot risk. The likely reason is that pills pass through the liver first. It's observational, and individual risk varies. Close with: 'Ask your clinician which route fits you, and don't stop or switch on your own.'
pieces.working_title: HRT Pill or Patch? The 1-in-1,000 Number That Matters
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 to drive traffic to the long video while the topic peaks (3–10 days). | fact-check: The same BMJ 2026 Danish nested case-control study as L1 (DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100688). The core claims are supported, but a 60-second format tends to drop nuance. Required: take the absolute figure from the paper and say it applies to women aged 50–69. Say it is observational. Say 'no overall increase' with patches/gels, not 'no risk'. Include an on-screen line saying don't change or stop HRT without talking to your clinician. Sources: https://bmjgroup.com/oral-menopausal-hormone-therapy-linked-to-higher-blood-clot-risk-in-legs-or-lungs-regardless-of-dose-or-duration/ ; https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-09-oral-menopausal-hormone-therapy-linked.html

pieces.topic: Scented cleaners + indoor ozone create billions of nanoparticles within minutes (Purdue, ACS Fall 2026)
pieces.angle: That 'fresh clean' scent comes from terpenes such as limonene and pinene, including in 'natural' essential-oil cleaners. Indoors they react with ozone, and in Purdue's house tests the tiny particles formed could deliver a lung dose similar to standing by a busy road within about 20 minutes. Three fixes: choose fragrance-free products, run an exhaust fan while cleaning, and don't use ozone-generating 'air purifiers'. Say clearly: this is early conference data, and scientists are still working out the health effects.
pieces.working_title: Your 'Clean' Smell Might Be Polluting Your Air
pieces.why: Brand-new, low competition, and fits the ongoing 'toxins at home' interest. Easy fixes make it shareable. Wording must stay cautious because it isn't peer-reviewed yet. | fact-check: Verified: Purdue (Brandon Boor's team), presented at ACS Fall 2026 (23–27 Aug, 'Healthy Indoor Spaces' symposium). Terpenes from scented cleaners, both conventional and essential-oil-based, react with indoor ozone to form nanocluster aerosol (<3 nm). The estimate is 100 billion to 10 trillion particles deposited in the airways within 20 minutes, and the respiratory dose was comparable to or greater than standing by a busy road. Fixes: this is conference data, not a peer-reviewed paper. 'Billions' is accurate (the dose is to the lungs, not particles 'created'). The researchers' own advice is unscented products, running exhaust fans, and avoiding ozone-generating devices while cleaning. 'Open a window' can let more outdoor ozone in, so swap it for 'ventilate / run an exhaust fan'. Health effects of these particles are not established, so avoid fear language. Sources: https://www.acs.org/pressroom/presspacs/2026/august/scented-cleaning-products-create-invisible-air-pollution.html ; https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1139679 ; http://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260925093152.htm

pieces.topic: Walking pace vs step count: under 5,000 brisk steps matched 10,000 slow ones for mortality risk (BJSM, 100k+ UK Biobank)
pieces.angle: 'Steps AND pace: a walking cheat sheet.' In 100k+ UK Biobank adults (BJSM 2026), people who walked under 5,000 steps a day but hit a brisker peak pace (>80 steps/min) had a death risk similar to people walking 5,000–7,500 steps at a slow ~60 steps/min. 7,500–10,000 steps was linked to the lowest risk at any pace. Slides: (1) the core finding; (2) cadence guide: ~60 = leisurely, >80 = brisker (study), ~100 = moderate intensity (other research); (3) 15-second self-test: count steps ×4 to check your current pace; (4) how step count and pace combine; (5) 'observational: a link, not proof'; (6) any pace beats none, so build up gradually. Drop the 8,500-steps note unless its source is verified. Title: 'The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?' is fine.
pieces.working_title: The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?
pieces.why: Evergreen fitness topic with a live news hook (National Geographic, MNT, Good Housekeeping this week). Simple, actionable numbers people save and share. | fact-check: Verified: BJSM, 8 Sep 2026, 103,684 UK Biobank participants, 7-day accelerometer. The topic's headline claim is WRONG. The study did not find that under 5,000 brisk steps matched 10,000 slow ones. It found that under 5,000 steps/day with a peak cadence above 80 steps/min carried a mortality risk comparable to 5,000–7,500 steps at ~60 steps/min. 7,500–10,000 steps was linked to the lowest risk at any pace, and at least 30 minutes a day at a brisker pace was linked to lower risk at any step count. Cadence slide: 60 and 80 spm come from the study. 100 spm is the widely used moderate-intensity threshold from other research (Tudor-Locke); label it that way and cite it separately. The 15-second ×4 self-test measures your current cadence, not the study's 'peak cadence', which is an average over your fastest minutes of the day. Say so. The earlier (May) 8,500-steps weight-maintenance result was not verified in this screen. Include it only if the writer confirms the primary source; otherwise drop it. Observational only. Sources: https://bmjgroup.com/different-daily-step-count-and-stepping-pace-combos-may-all-lower-risk-of-early-death/ ; https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/08/health/brisk-walking-pace-steps-wellness

pieces.topic: Stroke in younger adults: rising rates in ages 20–54 and the BE-FAST warning signs
pieces.angle: A public-service list: 'Stroke isn't just an old person's disease.' Include a slide per BE-FAST sign (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services), the main risk drivers (high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, smoking/drugs), and why younger adults wait too long to seek care. Quote the 'nearly doubled' figure only if the Neurology paper confirms it (the radar didn't link it). Otherwise say 'rising'.
pieces.working_title: Stroke Under 55: The 6 Signs That Mean Call Emergency Services Now
pieces.why: Evergreen life-saving content with a timely hook (2nd snapshot, CBS story). BE-FAST is exactly the kind of list people save and send to family.
